title: Examining the impact of food processing level and nutritional composition on energy intake
official: Examining the impact of food processing level and nutritional composition on energy intake: a randomised controlled trial
summary:
Background and study aims
The study is designed to examine the effect that different types of diet have on the amount of energy we consume each day. In particular, the study examines whether diets that are higher in ‘ultra-processed food’ result in us eating more than similar diets which are (or are not) matched to the ultra-processed diet for nutritional factors like fat, salt and sugar. The study is happening because research suggests ‘ultra-processed’ food may increase the amount of energy consumed per day, but at present it is unclear whether this is due to the typical nutritional profile of ultra-processed foods.

Who can participate?
Healthy adults aged 18-64 years can take part. For more detailed inclusion and eligibility criteria see other sections.

What does the study involve?
It is important to note that this study will require attending the University of Liverpool several times a day for three 4-day periods of Mondays to Thursdays. The study will involve being provided with breakfast, lunch and dinner to be consumed in our laboratory from Monday to Thursday for 3 weeks. You will also be provided with snacks to take away and consume during these days. If you are interested in the study, we can provide you with a detailed participant information sheet.  

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
There are no major anticipated risks. The presented foods will be commonly consumed in the UK and prepared adhering to Good Manufacturing Practice with appropriate risk analysis by individuals with a Level 2 Certificate in Food Safety and Hygiene. Because the study requires food consumption, we ask any potential participants with a food allergy not to participate. There are no intended benefits of taking part other than helping us develop a better understanding of diet and eating behaviour. If you complete all aspects of the study (three testing periods and relevant tasks) you will be reimbursed £300 for your participation in the form of a bank transfer (please note this can take up to 5 weeks).

Where is the study run from?
University of Liverpool (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
October 2026 to September 2027

Who is funding the study?
The Economic and Social Research Council (UK)

Who is the main contact?
Dr Victoria Norton (V.L.Norton@liverpool.ac.uk) or if unavailable, Prof Eric Robinson (eric.robinson@liv.ac.uk)
conditions: Effect of different dietary formulations on dietary intake (daily energy intake)

interventions.name: Participants will receive each diet for 4 days with a 1-week washout period in between to minimise carry-over effects. Cohorts of participants will be randomly allocated within a block-based design  (five blocks with six diet orders: ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, CBA) using a computer-generated sequence

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Aged 18 to 64 years
2. Body mass index (BMI) between 18.5 and 29.9 kg/m2
3. Read and speak English fluently
4. Willing to travel to the University of Liverpool
Exclusion criteria:
1. Dislike and/or not willing to consume study meals (reviewed during in-person screening and rate dislike [<4] on 9-point hedonic scale for any meal components)
2. Food allergies, intolerances or dietary requirements which cannot be adhered to due to study foods
3. Chronic conditions (e.g., diabetes, cancer, gastrointestinal disorders, kidney/liver disease, etc), poor oral health (including difficulties with eating/swallowing) or cognition impairments impacting memory (such as dementia)
4. History or current eating disorders and/or restrictive eating (including for religious reasons)
5. Following a weight-loss diet and/or not weight stable (5% change in past 3 months)
6. Current or recent smoker (including any tobacco, e-cigarettes, nicotine replacement therapy use in the past 3 months)
7. Pregnant or breastfeeding
8. Not regularly consuming three meals per day
9. Medication impacting study outcomes (including appetite, food intake, body weight, taste)
10. Unwilling to avoid drinking excessive amounts of alcohol (e.g., more than 14 units) per week during the three 4-day testing periods
11. Unwilling to refrain from too much strenuous exercise (e.g., >4 hours per week – that requires you to breathe hard and fast) during three 4-day testing periods and/or not follow an exercise routine similar to their habitual exercise habits during active study weeks
12. Participating in another research study involving food or alcohol consumption
13. Unable (or unwilling) to adhere to study requirements
14. Habitual intake considered implausible (24-hour recall)
